section_summary: Pages 144–175 conclude a secret study of the Japan Communist Party’s political, covert, and international potential, focusing on leadership, public support, labor organizing, infiltration, espionage, and alleged Soviet links. An October 1948 letter recommends the study to the State Department. A November despatch then begins an assessment of Japanese concern about communist activity in Hokkaido and Kyushu.

subfiles.title: The Communist Potential in Japan
subfiles.doc_type: secret despatch enclosure and analytical study
subfiles.from: Charles N. Spinks, United States Political Adviser’s Mission, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Assesses the Japan Communist Party’s political strength, covert organization, and international connections.
subfiles.summary: The concluding portion of the study argues that weak leadership and declining public appeal limit the party’s electoral prospects, while economic crisis could increase its support. It describes alleged communist fractions in unions, cultural groups, education, and government, together with strike planning, sabotage, and espionage apparatuses. The study attributes renewed international coordination to reported Cominform liaison and examines suspected Soviet training and intelligence support. Its conclusions emphasize the Occupation’s restraint on direct action and the potential effect of a future withdrawal.

subfiles.title: Letter forwarding The Communist Potential in Japan
subfiles.about: Forwards Spinks’s study and responds to Allison’s comments on communist support for an early peace conference.
subfiles.summary: Sebald recommends reading the study and suggests limiting its distribution.

subfiles.title: Japanese Concern over Communist Activity in Hokkaido and Kyushu
subfiles.from: United States Political Adviser for Japan, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Reports Japanese concern about communist strength in Hokkaido and Kyushu after the capture of Mukden.
subfiles.summary: The despatch compares estimated party membership and population ratios in Hokkaido, Kyushu, Tokyo, and Osaka. It describes Hokkaido’s organized communist activity, railway dispute tactics, espionage, and reported warnings of a Soviet seizure. The document continues beyond page 178.
